newsitem.title: USA: Arguments open in New Jersey "Megan's law" trial.
newsitem.headline: Arguments open in New Jersey "Megan's law" trial.

text.p: Opening arguments began Monday in the trial of the man accused of raping and killing a 7-year-old girl in a case that led to the adoption of federal and state laws requiring that communities be notified of the presence of convicted sex offenders.

Authorities alleged that in July 1994, twice-convicted sex offender Jesse Timmendequas, 35, was living in Hamilton Township, a working-class suburb of Trenton, N.J., when he lured Megan Kanka into his home to see a puppy, then raped her and strangled her.
His neighbours did not know of his past offences.
As the trial opened Monday with the girl's parents sitting in the Mercer County courtroom, prosecutor Kathryn Flicker pointed to the defendant and said, "That man would change their lives forever."
She said Megan Kanka tried to scream and fight her way out of the accused man's house after the attack.
The parents, Maureen and Richard Kanka, were expected to be among the first to testify before Judge Andrew Smithson.
The parents helped win legislative changes in more than six states. President Clinton signed a federal version of "Megan's Law" last year and 44 states have variations of the law on their books.
The trial was expected to last about six weeks, shorter than the laborious jury selection, which took more than two months.
During the campaign to change the law, the criminal record of the accused killer was widely discussed. Timmendequas was convicted in the assaults on two other New Jersey girls in 1980 and 1981.

Megan's Law in New Jersey requires sex offenders to register with police and empowers prosecutors to screen them for risk to the public, with the public being told about those assessed as posing the highest risk. The public notification is under legal challenge in the federal courts.
The defence said the extensive publicity linking the crime to the political campaign made it necessary to screen jurors for knowledge of the new law.

Jurors were selected from semi-rural Hunterdon County to lessen the chance that pre-trial publicity would taint the trial. The jurors were being bused the 20 miles between Flemington in Hunterdon County and the Mercer County Court in Trenton, the state capital.
